A believing woman mourns no one beyond three days except her husband, four months and ten days, which the Prophet contrasted with a pre-Islamic year when refusing a widow collyrium.
A woman mourns no one beyond three days except her husband, four months and ten days, without collyrium, perfume or dyed garments, save a little incense after her courses.
Uwaimir asked about a man finding another with his wife; under the revealed verses spouses swore four oaths and a fifth curse, were separated, and the dower stayed hers.
After mutual cursing, children were born as the Prophet foretold or resembling the accused man; Ibn Abbas said the Prophet's words on stoning without evidence concerned another woman.
Sa'd b. Ubada, ready to kill a man found with his wife, was told to bring four witnesses; the Prophet called himself more jealous than Sa'd, and Allah more so.
A dark child, like a dusky camel among red ones, may reflect a reverted strain, the Prophet told a man wanting to disown his son, and did not permit it.
A co-owner freeing his share frees the slave fully if he can pay partners a fair price; otherwise the slave is partly freed or works, not overburdened, for the rest.
Barira's owners would sell her only keeping her wala; the Prophet said wala is the freer's and conditions outside Allah's Book are void; freed, she chose to leave her husband.
Selling or gifting the wala is forbidden, and whoever takes a freed slave as ally without his former master's consent bears the curse of Allah, the angels and all mankind.
Whoever frees a Muslim slave, Allah frees from the Fire a limb of his for every limb of the slave; on hearing this Ali b. Husain freed a costly slave.
A son cannot repay what he owes his father unless he finds him a slave, buys him and sets him free.
The Prophet forbade the sales called mulamasa and munabadha, closing a deal by touching or throwing a garment without inspecting it, and also two ways of dressing.
The Prophet forbade sales settled by throwing a pebble, sales involving uncertainty, and habal al-habala, a sale deferred until a she-camel's offspring is born and itself becomes pregnant.
A Muslim must not enter a sale while his brother is bargaining, nor propose marriage over his brother's proposal unless he permits it.
The Prophet forbade meeting caravans on the way, outbidding, buying against a brother, a townsman selling for a desert dweller, tying animals' udders, and a woman seeking her sister's divorce.
Merchandise and traders must not be met on the way before they reach the market; a seller bought from that way may cancel the sale on reaching it.
A townsman must not sell on behalf of a man from the desert, even his brother or father; Ibn Abbas explained it as acting as his broker.
Whoever buys a goat or she-camel whose udder was tied up may keep it after milking, or return it within three days with a sa' of dates, not wheat.
Whoever buys foodgrain must not resell it before taking possession and measuring it; people were beaten for reselling on the spot, and Marwan stopped sales made by documents.
The Prophet forbade selling a heap of dates of unknown weight for a known measure of dates.
Both parties to a sale may annul it until they separate, unless an option was agreed; honest, open dealing is blessed, while lying and concealment wipe out the blessing.
A man who was cheated in sales was told by the Prophet to say, when making a deal, that there should be no deception.
The Prophet forbade seller and buyer to trade fruit before its good condition is clear, when it turns red or yellow, is fit to eat and safe from blight.
While forbidding fresh dates on the tree for dry dates, the Prophet allowed the 'ariyya, by which a household gives measured dry dates for fresh dates to eat.
Selling fresh dates for dry dates is riba and muzabana, except for families given a tree or two as 'ariyya, allowed for up to five wasqs or less.
The Prophet forbade muzabana: selling fresh dates on the tree for dry dates, grapes for raisins, or standing crops for grain, by measure or by estimate.
When pollinated palms are sold their fruit belongs to the seller, and when a slave is sold his property belongs to the seller, unless the buyer stipulates otherwise.
The Prophet forbade muhaqala, muzabana, mukhabara, sales years ahead and fruit before it ripens, and sales except for dinars and dirhams, 'araya excepted; Jabir explained the terms.
The Prophet forbade renting out land or taking a share of its crop: an owner should cultivate it himself, lend it free to his brother, or keep it.
The Prophet forbade renting land or selling its produce years ahead, and muzabana and muhaqala, the latter explained as renting land; an owner should cultivate or lend it.
Ibn Umar rented out his land until Rafi b. Khadij told him, from his uncles, that the Prophet had forbidden renting land, and then he gave it up.
Rafi b. Khadij's uncle conveyed the Prophet's ban on renting land for a third or quarter of its crop or measured grain: cultivate it, have it cultivated, or keep it.
Renting land for gold or silver is allowed; what was forbidden was letting land for the crop of one plot, which might fail, and sharecropping, rent being permitted.
Ibn Abbas held that the Prophet did not forbid renting land outright, but said lending it to one's brother is better than taking a fixed return from it.
The Prophet let Khaibar's Jews work its land and palms for half the produce while he wished; later Umar offered the Prophet's wives land or wasqs and expelled the Jews.
Whatever people, beasts or birds eat from what a Muslim plants or sows, or is stolen from it, counts as charity for him.
If fruit sold to a brother is struck by calamity the seller may take nothing; the Prophet ordered deductions for such loss and forbade selling dates before they ripen.
Creditors were told to take what a ruined debtor had, one who swore against granting remission relented, and at the Prophet's sign Ka'b remitted half of a debt.
A seller who finds his goods still intact with a buyer who has become insolvent has more right to them than any other creditor.
Allah forgave a rich man of earlier times who gave respite to insolvent debtors and leniency to the solvent; whoever wants safety on Resurrection Day should grant respite or remit.
